title: Data Modeling for Scale
summary: At scale, data models optimize for access patterns and partition keys, not only normalization purity. Good models make hot queries local and cheap; bad models force scatter-gather forever.

sections.title: Access patterns first
paragraphs: List reads/writes with QPS and latency. Model around those paths. In partitioned stores, the partition key is the most important decision.

sections.title: Normalization vs denormalization
paragraphs: Normalize to protect write integrity; denormalize to protect read latency. Duplication requires clear update rules — CDC and application dual updates are options with different failure modes.

sections.title: Keys and hotspots
paragraphs: Monotonic keys create write hotspots. High cardinality + even access is ideal. Tenant+time composites need care to avoid skew.

sections.title: Evolving schemas
paragraphs: Expand/contract migrations, dual writes, and backfills. Avoid locking migrations on huge tables without a plan.

deepDive.title: Data Modeling for Scale — Operations
paragraphs: Operating Data Modeling for Scale in production means defining SLIs before tuning knobs, knowing amplification costs, and rehearsing failure modes.
Prefer reversible changes, feature flags, and canaries. Measure p50/p99 and error rate under load that matches production skew.
bullets: Define capacity from the scarcest resource
Keep rollback cheaper than forward repair when possible

deepDive.title: Data Modeling for Scale — Failure modes
paragraphs: Common failures around Data Modeling for Scale include overload, partial dependency outages, and silent correctness bugs that pass happy-path tests.
Inject faults in staging: latency, loss, clock skew, and disk full. Verify alerts fire and degradation is intentional.

expert.title: Data Modeling for Scale — Expert notes
paragraphs: At the expert level, Data Modeling for Scale intersects multi-region consistency, cost envelopes, and organizational constraints (team ownership, on-call load).
Write down the non-goals. Many outages come from optimizing a metric that was never the product requirement.

practices: Write access patterns before ER diagrams
pitfalls: Pretty schemas that cannot be sharded
keyTakeaways: Scale models start from access paths
whyItMatters: You cannot fix a bad key choice with more hardware alone.
reflectionQuestions: What is the partition key for your hottest entity?
numbersToKnow: Know your p99 latency budget before adding hops
Peak load ≠ average load — plan headroom (often 2–3×)
Cross-region RTT is often ~50–150ms one way
